pages.h1: Best virtual event platforms, compared by use case
pages.definition: The best virtual event platform is the one that fits the event: Zoom or Microsoft Teams for internal meetings and simple webinars, ON24 or Goldcast for marketing webinars that feed a CRM, Cvent or Bizzabo for conferences with registration and sponsors, and StreamYard for branded livestreams. Choose on audience size, interaction, integrations and who runs it live.
facts: Ten platforms compared below, from self-serve streaming studios to enterprise event suites.

Three cost models: per-host licences sized by attendee capacity (Zoom Webinars), self-serve monthly plans (StreamYard, Livestorm), and annual contracts quoted by sales (ON24, Cvent, Bizzabo, Goldcast).
The platform is not the production. Someone still has to own the run of show, rehearse speakers and keep a backup stream ready.
Moderated webinars: $2,500 to $7,500 per production (West Peek Productions published range, directional, not a fixed quote).
Executive summits, online conferences and hybrid productions: $10,000 to $50,000 and above (West Peek Productions published range).
West Peek Productions does not sell event software. It produces events on the platform you choose and can help you choose it.

sections.h2: How do you compare virtual event platforms?

blocks.p: Score each shortlisted platform against the event you are actually running, not against a feature list. These seven criteria decide most choices:

ol: Audience and access: internal sign-on, public registration, paid tickets, or invite-only.
Scale: the attendee cap of the licence tier and how many people will be on stage at once.
Interaction: Q&A, polls, chat, breakouts, networking and sponsor booths you genuinely need.
Integrations: HubSpot, Salesforce or Marketo sync if leads matter; single sign-on if it is internal.
Production model: browser studio only, or RTMP input from an external encoder such as vMix or OBS for broadcast-quality graphics.
Accessibility and replay: live captions, recording, an on-demand library and transcript.
Total cost: licence plus production plus the staff hours to run it, compared across the whole year.

sections.h2: Which platform fits webinars, summits, conferences and hybrid events?

ul: Webinars: Zoom Webinars, Microsoft Teams webinars, ON24, Goldcast, Livestorm.
Multi-session summits: Goldcast, RingCentral Events, Airmeet, Zoom Events.
Conferences with sponsors and registration: Cvent, Bizzabo, Swapcard, Webex Events.
Hybrid events: Cvent, Bizzabo, Webex Events, Swapcard, with on-site AV feeding the stream (see the hybrid event platform guide).
Branded livestreams and town halls on social channels: StreamYard, Restream, Vimeo.

faq.q: What is the best virtual event platform?
faq.a: There is no single best platform. Zoom and Microsoft Teams suit internal events and simple webinars, ON24 and Goldcast suit marketing webinar programmes, Cvent and Bizzabo suit conferences with sponsors and registration, and StreamYard suits branded livestreams. Match the platform to audience size, interaction and integrations.

faq.q: What is a virtual event platform?
faq.a: A virtual event platform is software that hosts an online event: registration, a live stage or webinar room, speaker backstage, attendee Q&A, polls and chat, sometimes networking and sponsor booths, then a recording and analytics. It does not plan or run the show; that is production.

faq.q: What are the best platforms for virtual conferences?
faq.a: For multi-track conferences with registration, agendas and sponsors, Cvent, Bizzabo, Swapcard and Webex Events are the usual shortlist. For lighter multi-session summits, Goldcast, RingCentral Events, Airmeet and Zoom Events cost less and are faster to set up.

faq.q: What are the best hybrid event platforms?

Platform vendor services suit teams committed to one platform, AV companies suit camera-heavy hybrid shows, event agencies suit in-person-led events, and producers such as West Peek Productions suit high-stakes online events that need a run of show, rehearsal and a backup plan.

pages.description: Hybrid event platform guide: what the software does, the platforms worth shortlisting, and what hybrid event production adds, with published price ranges.
pages.h1: Hybrid event platforms: what they do and which to choose
pages.definition: A hybrid event platform is software that runs one event for an in-person and an online audience at once: registration, a live stream of the room, remote speakers, shared Q&A and polls, networking and replay. Cvent, Bizzabo, Swapcard, Webex Events and Zoom Events are common choices; production is what makes both audiences feel included.
facts: Platform and production are two purchases: the platform is software; production is the crew, cameras, encoder, run of show and backup stream.
Plan a hybrid conference six to eight weeks out; lock the venue AV and the platform before the agenda is final.
Executive summits, online conferences and hybrid productions: $10,000 to $50,000 and above (West Peek Productions published range).
West Peek Productions does not sell event software. It produces events on the platform you choose and can help you choose it.

sections.h2: What does a hybrid event platform do?

ul: Registration and ticketing for in-person and online attendees in one list.
A live stream of the main stage, with captions and a recording.
Remote speakers joining the room through a backstage.
One Q&A and polling queue shared by the room and the online audience.
Networking, meeting booking and sponsor pages for both audiences.
On-site check-in and badges, an event app, and an on-demand library afterwards.

sections.h2: What does hybrid event production add to the platform?

blocks.p: The platform carries the stream; it does not create it. Hybrid event production supplies everything between the room and the online audience:

ul: Cameras and room audio fed into an encoder, so remote viewers see and hear the stage properly.
A dedicated online host who speaks to the remote audience and brings their questions into the room.
Remote speaker rehearsal on the real setup before the day.
One run of show with cues for the room and the stream.
A backup stream and a second internet connection.
Captions, the recording and edited replays.

sections.h2: How much does hybrid event production cost?

blocks.p: West Peek Productions publishes a range of $10,000 to $50,000 and above for hybrid productions, summits and online conferences. The ranges are directional, not fixed quotes. What moves the number:

ul: Number of cameras and rooms streamed.
Event days and rehearsal days.
Venue AV already in place versus brought in.
Remote speakers, interpreters and caption languages.
Edited replays and clips after the event.

sections.h2: Should you choose the platform or the producer first?

blocks.p: Bring the producer in first, or at the same time. The producer turns your goals into platform requirements (audience size, interaction, integrations, on-site check-in) and tests the shortlist against them, so you do not pay for a platform that cannot carry the show you are planning. West Peek Productions does that platform selection as part of a production, then produces the event on the platform you choose. For a broader comparison, see the best virtual event platforms.

faq.q: What is a hybrid event platform?
faq.a: A hybrid event platform is software that serves an in-person and an online audience at the same event: shared registration, a streamed stage, remote speakers, one Q&A queue, networking and replay. Common examples are Cvent, Bizzabo, Swapcard, Webex Events and Zoom Events.

faq.q: What is hybrid event production?
faq.a: Hybrid event production is the crew and planning that put an in-person event in front of an online audience: cameras, room audio, an encoder, an online host, remote speaker rehearsal, a run of show for both audiences and a backup stream. It runs on whichever platform you choose.

faq.q: Which platform is best for hybrid events?
faq.a: For large conferences, Cvent or Bizzabo; for networking-led events, Swapcard; for Cisco companies, Webex Events; for budget-conscious events with a Zoom-familiar audience, Zoom Events. Choose after you know audience size, interaction and on-site needs.

faq.q: Do you need a hybrid events company or just a platform?
faq.a: You need both. The platform is software you license; a hybrid events company provides the cameras, crew, online host, rehearsal and backup stream that make the online half feel like part of the event rather than a camera at the back of the room.

faq.q: How far ahead should you plan a hybrid event?
faq.a: Six to eight weeks for a hybrid conference: platform and venue AV in weeks one and two, agenda and speakers by week four, remote speaker rehearsals in the final week, and a full technical rehearsal on the day before.

pages.description: Content marketing operations services explained: the seven-stage workflow, deliverables, where AI content operations fits, and agency vs in-house options.
pages.h1: Content marketing operations: the workflow behind every piece
pages.definition: Content marketing operations is the system that turns content requests into published, measured work: intake and briefs, a production calendar, writing and design, review and legal approval, publishing, distribution and reporting. AI content operations adds drafting, repurposing and tagging inside that workflow, with a human editor approving everything that ships.
facts: Seven stages, each with one owner and one output: intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing, reporting.
Common tools: Asana, Monday.com or Airtable for the calendar; Google Docs or Notion for briefs; WordPress, Webflow or HubSpot for publishing; GA4 and HubSpot for reporting.
A realistic cycle for a long-form article is five to ten working days from approved brief to publish, most of it in review.
West Peek Productions scopes content operations work per engagement; it does not publish a fixed price. Send the scope for a quote.

sections.h2: What does content marketing operations include?

ol: Intake: one request form, so work is not commissioned in chat threads.
Brief: audience, goal, key message, format, owner and due date, approved before anyone writes.
Production: writing, design and video on a shared calendar with capacity limits.
Review: an editor checks against the brief, the style guide and a QA checklist.
Approval: named approvers, including legal or compliance where needed, with a deadline for feedback.
Publishing and distribution: a publishing checklist for SEO fields, links, tracking and channel versions.
Reporting: monthly numbers on output, cycle time and what the content influenced.

sections.h2: What do content operation services deliver?

ul: An intake form and a brief template.
An editorial calendar with owners and capacity.
A RACI that says who writes, reviews and approves.
A style guide and QA checklist.
A publishing checklist and a reuse plan for each long piece.
A reporting dashboard.
An AI usage policy: which steps may use AI, and who approves the output.

Produce a first draft from an approved brief
Rewrite for voice, accuracy and claims
Cut a webinar or article into posts, emails and clips
Approve every version before it ships
Suggest titles, descriptions, tags and alt text
Check them against the page and the brand
Pull the numbers and draft the summary

Best when

sections.h2: How do you measure content operations?

ul: Cycle time from approved brief to published.
Throughput: pieces published per month against plan.
Revision rounds per piece.
On-time rate against the calendar.
Reuse: derivative assets per long-form piece.
Pipeline or sign-ups influenced by content.

faq.q: What is content marketing operations?
faq.a: Content marketing operations is the workflow, roles and tools that move content from request to published and measured: intake, briefs, a production calendar, review and approval, publishing, distribution and reporting.

faq.q: What do content marketing operation services include?
faq.a: Typically an intake form and brief template, an editorial calendar with owners, a RACI for review and approval, a style guide and QA checklist, a publishing checklist, a reporting dashboard and an AI usage policy, plus the people to run them if you hire an agency.

faq.q: What is AI content operations?
faq.a: AI content operations uses AI tools at named steps of the content workflow, such as research summaries, first drafts, repurposing and metadata, while an editor approves every output before it is published.

faq.q: What does an agency content operations team do?
faq.a: It designs the content workflow and runs it: intake, briefs, scheduling, production, review, publishing and reporting, with your team approving the work at agreed points.

faq.q: What does a marketing content operation workflow look like?
faq.a: Seven stages with one owner each: intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing and distribution, and reporting. Work moves forward only when the previous stage's output is approved.

pages.title: Virtual Event Checklist: How to Host a Virtual Event
pages.description: A numbered virtual event checklist from goal to replay, the planning timeline in weeks, and how to host a virtual event on the day without improvising.
pages.h1: Virtual event checklist: how to host a virtual event, step by step
pages.definition: A virtual event checklist is the ordered list of decisions and tasks that takes an online event from idea to replay: goal and audience, date and platform, speakers and run of show, registration and promotion, rehearsal and backups, the live show, then recording, follow-up and reporting. Start six to eight weeks out for a summit.
facts: Lead time: six to eight weeks for a summit or conference, three to four weeks for a webinar.
One full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before, and a technical check 60 minutes before going live.
Send the replay within 24 to 48 hours, while attendees still remember the event.
Moderated webinars: $2,500 to $7,500 per production (West Peek Productions published range, directional, not a fixed quote).

sections.h2: What goes on a virtual event checklist?

ol: Write the goal and the one number that says it worked (registrations, attendance, pipeline, sign-ups).
Define the audience and the time zone you are planning for.
Pick the format: webinar, panel, multi-session summit or hybrid.
Set the date, avoiding holidays and competing events.
Choose the platform against audience size, interaction and integrations.
Confirm speakers and moderator, with a short brief for each.
Draft the run of show minute by minute, with an owner for every cue.
Build the registration page and confirmation emails.
Plan promotion: email, social, partners and speaker posts, with dates.
Collect slides and videos by a firm deadline.
Design branded slides, lower thirds and holding screens.
Write the Q&A and poll plan, including two seeded questions.
Arrange captions and accessibility needs.
Set up a backup: a second presenter machine, a second connection and a backup stream link.
Send speaker kits: camera, microphone, lighting and joining instructions.
Run a technical check with every speaker on their own setup.
Hold a full rehearsal on the real platform, two to five days before.
Send reminders one day and one hour before.
Open the backstage 60 minutes before and test audio, video and slides.
Run the show to the run of show, with one person calling cues.
Moderate chat and Q&A, and keep time.
Record the session and note timestamps for clips.
Send the replay and resources within 24 to 48 hours.
Follow up with attendees and no-shows separately.
Report against the goal, and write down what to change next time.

sections.h2: What is a realistic virtual event planning timeline?

head: When
What to lock
rows: Goal, audience, format, date, platform and budget
Speakers confirmed, registration page live, promotion plan
Run of show drafted, branded assets in design, speaker kits sent
Slides and videos collected, Q&A and poll plan, captions booked
Speaker technical checks, backup setup tested
Full rehearsal on the real platform
Backstage open 60 minutes early, show called to the run of show

sections.h2: How do you host a virtual event on the day?

ul: One producer calls cues; speakers only present.
Keep a written run of show open for everyone backstage.
Have a moderator for chat and Q&A, separate from the host.
Start on time with a holding screen and music, not a silent room.
Know in advance who switches to the backup if the main stream fails.

sections.h2: When is it worth getting help hosting a virtual event?

blocks.p: When the event carries revenue, investor trust or executive visibility, or has several speakers, sponsors or a hybrid room. West Peek Productions produces webinars from $2,500 to $7,500 and summits, conferences and hybrid events from $10,000, owning the run of show, rehearsal and backup so nothing important is improvised.

faq.q: What should be on a virtual event checklist?
faq.a: Goal and audience, format and date, platform, speakers and run of show, registration and promotion, branded assets, Q&A and polls, captions, a backup plan, speaker technical checks, a full rehearsal, the live show, the recording, follow-up and a report.

faq.q: How do you host a virtual event?
faq.a: Set a goal, pick the format and platform, confirm speakers, write a run of show, open registration and promote it, rehearse on the real platform, run the show with one person calling cues and a moderator on Q&A, then send the replay and follow up within 48 hours.
faq.from_query: how to host a virtual event

faq.q: What is a good virtual event planning timeline?
faq.a: Six to eight weeks for a summit: lock goal, platform and date first, speakers and registration by week five, run of show and assets by week three, technical checks in the final week and a full rehearsal two to five days before. A webinar needs three to four weeks.

faq.q: What goes on a virtual event production checklist?
faq.a: The production items: run of show with cue owners, platform and registration setup, branded graphics, speaker kits and technical checks, captions, backup machine, connection and stream, a full rehearsal, recording and edited replay.

faq.q: What is the best way to host a virtual event?
faq.a: Separate the roles: a host who presents, a producer who calls cues, and a moderator who handles chat and Q&A. Rehearse on the real platform and agree in advance who switches to the backup if something fails.
